mainTopic: דרוסה: which predators make an animal a טריפה, how the clawing must happen, and doubtful clawing (ספק דרוסה)
overview: The גמרא explains that whether a cat or a weasel has דרוסה depends on the victim: birds, adult sheep, or kids and lambs. רב אשי asks whether non-kosher birds other than the hawk have דרוסה. The answer is yes, and the hawk is named in the משנה because it is stronger. Two versions follow about the fox, and they agree that a cat has דרוסה and a dog does not. אביי lists four conditions for real דרוסה: front leg, claw, on purpose, and a living attacker. He adds that the venom enters only when the claws are pulled out. רב rules that a claw found in an ox's back after a lion came in is only a ספק דרוסה, so the ox is permitted, and אביי narrows this ruling. Finally the גמרא brings the מחלוקת between רב and שמואל about ספק דרוסה and starts listing cases where everyone agrees we do not worry. That list continues on the next amud.

steps.title: First question: does a cat have the power of clawing?
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא asks רב whether a cat's clawing makes an animal a טריפה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does a cat have דרוסה, or does a cat not have דרוסה?
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא asks רב whether a cat counts as a predator whose clawing makes its victim a טריפה. This sets up רב's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דרוסה is a special kind of attack: a predator claws its prey and releases venom that makes the victim a טריפה. Not every animal is strong enough to do this. The question is whether a cat is.

keyTerms.meaning: Clawing by a predator, which makes the victim a טריפה
An animal with a fatal injury, forbidden to eat even if slaughtered properly

phrases.english: Does a cat have clawing?
Or does a cat not have clawing?

steps.triggerLanguage: יֵשׁ דְּרוּסָה לְחָתוּל אוֹ אֵין דְּרוּסָה לְחָתוּל
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a cat's clawing makes an animal a טריפה

steps.title: רב answers: even a weasel has clawing
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that even a weasel, which is smaller than a cat, has דרוסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Even a weasel has דרוסה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers yes, and goes further: even the weaker weasel has דרוסה, so a cat certainly does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'even' shows a step up in strength. If the smaller weasel can do דרוסה, the bigger cat obviously can.

keyTerms.meaning: Weasel, a smaller animal than a cat

phrases.english: He said to him:
Even a weasel has clawing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַף לְחוּלְדָּה יֵשׁ דְּרוּסָה
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. Even a weasel has דרוסה, so a cat certainly does.

steps.title: Second question: does a weasel have the power of clawing?
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא now asks the same question about a weasel.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does a weasel have דרוסה, or does a weasel not have דרוסה?
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא asks a second question, this time about the weasel. This sets up another answer from רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same kind of question, now about the weasel. רב's answer will seem to clash with his first one, and the גמרא resolves this in step 7 by showing each answer was about a different victim.

keyTerms.meaning: There is not / does not have

phrases.english: Does a weasel have clawing?
Or does a weasel not have clawing?

steps.triggerLanguage: יֵשׁ דְּרוּסָה לְחוּלְדָּה אוֹ אֵין דְּרוּסָה לְחוּלְדָּה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a weasel's clawing makes an animal a טריפה

steps.title: רב answers: even a cat has no clawing
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that even a cat, which is stronger than a weasel, has no דרוסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Even a cat does not have דרוסה.
steps.whatsHappening: This time רב says no, and goes further: even the stronger cat does not have דרוסה, so a weasel certainly does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer looks like the exact opposite of step 2. There, even a weasel had דרוסה. Here, even a cat does not. The גמרא will settle this in step 7.

keyTerms.meaning: Has no clawing power; its attack does not make the victim a טריפה

steps.confusionAlert: Do not decide that רב changed his mind. The גמרא will show that each answer was about a different kind of victim.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Even a cat does not have clawing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַף לְחָתוּל אֵין דְּרוּסָה
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No. Even a cat has no דרוסה, so a weasel certainly does not.

steps.title: Third question: what about both the cat and the weasel?
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא asks about the cat and the weasel together.
steps.simpleTranslation: A cat and a weasel: do they have דרוסה, or do they not have דרוסה?
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא asks a third question, covering both animals at once. This sets up a third answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Asking about both together invites an answer that compares the two animals directly.

phrases.english: A cat and a weasel,
do they have clawing
or do they not have clawing?

steps.triggerLanguage: לְחָתוּל וּלְחוּלְדָּה יֵשׁ לָהֶן דְּרוּסָה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the cat and the weasel each have דרוסה

steps.title: רב answers: a cat yes, a weasel no
steps.stepSummary: רב splits the two: a cat has דרוסה, a weasel does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: A cat has דרוסה; a weasel does not have דרוסה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב gives a middle answer. The cat has דרוסה, but the weasel does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there are three answers that do not match. In step 2 both animals have דרוסה. In step 4 neither does. In step 6 only the cat does. This sets up the גמרא's resolution.

keyTerms.meaning: Cat yes, weasel no: the split answer

phrases.english: He said to him:
A cat has clawing;
a weasel does not have clawing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ לְחָתוּל יֵשׁ דְּרוּסָה לְחוּלְדָּה אֵין דְּרוּסָה
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A cat has דרוסה; a weasel does not.

steps.title: Each answer depends on the size of the victim
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves the three answers by matching each one to a different victim: birds, adult sheep, or kids and lambs.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. When רב said 'even a weasel has דרוסה,' he was talking about birds. When he said 'even a cat has no דרוסה,' he was talking about big adult sheep. When he said 'a cat has, a weasel has not,' he was talking about young goats and lambs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the three answers do not really contradict each other. Each one was about a different kind of victim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Whether a predator has דרוסה depends on how strong it is compared to its victim. Birds are small, so even a weasel can do דרוסה to them. Adult sheep are big, so not even a cat can. Kids and lambs are in the middle, so a cat can and a weasel cannot.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; the contradiction is resolved

steps.whatToRemember: דרוסה is not a fixed trait of the predator. It depends on the predator compared to its victim. A weasel has דרוסה on birds. A cat has דרוסה on kids and lambs. Neither has דרוסה on adult sheep.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a practical rule: to decide whether an attacked animal is a טריפה, you must look at both the attacker and the size of the victim.

phrases.english: And it is not difficult:
phrases.notes: The question was never asked out loud. The גמרא assumes you noticed that רב's three answers don't match.

phrases.english: That which he said to him,
'Even a weasel has clawing' – was about birds;
that which he said to him,
'Even a cat does not have clawing' –
was about big sheep;
that which he said to him,
'A cat has clawing,
a weasel does not have clawing' –
was about kids and lambs.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא קַשְׁיָא הָא דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the hidden contradiction among רב's three answers
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different cases (אוקימתא): each answer applies to a different victim
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב's answers seem to contradict each other about the cat and the weasel.
steps.terutzMaskana: Weasel on birds: יש דרוסה. Cat or weasel on adult sheep: אין דרוסה. Cat on kids and lambs: יש דרוסה. Weasel on kids and lambs: אין דרוסה.

steps.title: רב אשי asks about other non-kosher birds
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי asks whether non-kosher birds other than the hawk also have דרוסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי asked: Do other non-kosher birds have דרוסה, or do they not have דרוסה?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins. The משנה said a bird clawed by a hawk is a טריפה, and רב אשי asks whether other non-kosher birds count too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה names only the hawk. The question is whether the hawk is just one example of the non-kosher birds of prey, or whether only the hawk has this power.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises a question he is unsure about

phrases.english: Rav Ashi raised a question:
Other non-kosher birds,
do they have clawing
or do they not have clawing?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַב אָשֵׁי שְׁאָר עוֹפוֹת טְמֵאִין
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether non-kosher birds other than the hawk make a bird a טריפה through דרוסה

steps.title: רב הלל reports רב כהנא's answer: yes
steps.stepSummary: רב הלל tells רב אשי that רב כהנא ruled that other non-kosher birds have דרוסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הלל said to רב אשי: When we were in רב כהנא's study hall, he said that other non-kosher birds do have דרוסה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הלל answers רב אשי's question by passing on a ruling he heard from רב כהנא: yes, other non-kosher birds have דרוסה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer comes from a tradition, not from logic. רב הלל heard it himself in רב כהנא's study hall. So the hawk in the משנה is just one example.

keyTerms.meaning: The study hall of a teacher

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב כהנא, all non-kosher birds of prey, not only the hawk, have דרוסה.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב הִלֵּל לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Hillel said to Rav Ashi:
When we were in the study hall of Rav Kahana,
he said:
Other non-kosher birds
do have clawing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב הִלֵּל לְרַב אָשֵׁי כִּי הֲוֵינַן בֵּי רַב כָּהֲנָא
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. Based on רב כהנא's ruling, other non-kosher birds also have דרוסה.

steps.title: The משנה mentions only the hawk
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב כהנא's ruling. The משנה names only the נץ (hawk) as clawing a small bird.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the משנה says 'clawed by a hawk, in a small bird.' That sounds like only a hawk can do this!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ruling from Step 9 that other non-kosher birds also have דרוסה. It quotes our משנה, which mentions only the hawk.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every non-kosher bird of prey had דרוסה, why would the משנה name only the נץ? The specific wording seems to suggest that the hawk alone counts.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But isn't it so...?', the opening of a challenge

phrases.english: But didn't we learn in the mishna:
'Or clawed by a hawk, in the case of a small bird'!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאֲנַן תְּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב כהנא's ruling reported in Step 9
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that other non-kosher birds have דרוסה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה names only the hawk, which suggests that other birds do not count

steps.title: The hawk can harm a bird its own size
steps.stepSummary: The hawk's דרוסה works even on a bird as big as itself. Other birds' דרוסה works only on smaller birds.
steps.simpleTranslation: The hawk's clawing counts even on a bird its own size. The other birds' clawing counts only on a bird smaller than them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Other birds do have דרוסה, but the hawk is stronger, so the משנה mentions it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference is not whether a bird has דרוסה at all. It is how big a victim its דרוסה works on. The hawk works even on an equal-sized bird, while the others only work on smaller ones. That extra power is why the משנה names the hawk.

keyTerms.meaning: On one like itself, meaning the same size

phrases.english: Clawing by a hawk counts even on one like itself,
phrases.notes: 'Like itself' means a bird the same size as the hawk.

phrases.english: and those others only on one smaller than them.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּרוּסַת הָנֵץ בְּדִכְוָותֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 10
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing by the size of the victim
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only the hawk has דרוסה, because the משנה names only it
steps.terutzMaskana: All birds of prey have דרוסה; the hawk is named because it works even on an equal-sized bird

steps.title: Second version: the hawk can harm even a bigger bird
steps.stepSummary: Another version moves each line up one size. The hawk's דרוסה works even on a bigger bird, and the other birds' דרוסה works on birds their own size.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: the hawk's clawing counts even on a bird bigger than it, and the others' clawing counts on a bird their own size.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the same answer, with each size limit raised by one step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea stays the same: the hawk is stronger than other birds of prey. Only the size cut-off changes. In this version, other birds can harm a bird their own size, and the hawk can harm even a bigger one.

phrases.english: And there are those who say:
Clawing by a hawk counts even on one bigger than it,
and those others on one like themselves.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second version of the answer in Step 11
steps.terutzResolutionType: Same distinction, with the size limits moved
steps.terutzMaskana: The hawk can harm even a bigger bird; other birds can harm a bird their own size

steps.title: A fox has no דרוסה
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא, quoting רב שימי בר אשי, rules that a fox's clawing does not make an animal a טריפה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said in the name of רב שימי בר אשי: a fox does not have דרוסה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic: whether a fox counts as an animal with deadly clawing. רב כהנא says it does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far the סוגיא has looked at cats, weasels, and birds. Now a new animal is added. According to this ruling, if a fox claws a sheep, the sheep does not become a טריפה.

keyTerms.meaning: Deadly clawing by a predator, which makes the victim a טְרֵפָה

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Kahana said in the name of Rav Shimi bar Ashi:
A fox does not have clawing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about the fox
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A fox's clawing does not make an animal a טריפה

steps.title: A story where the fox did count
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reported a real case. A fox clawed a sheep, and the חכמים ruled that it was דרוסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really? But רב דימי came and said: a fox once clawed a sheep in the bathhouse of בית היני, and the חכמים said it counts as דרוסה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב כהנא's ruling with a real case from ארץ ישראל, where the חכמים treated a fox's clawing as real דרוסה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An actual ruling by the חכמים is strong evidence. If they called a fox's clawing דרוסה, then רב כהנא's ruling that a fox has no דרוסה seems to be wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Is that so?', expressing doubt before a challenge

phrases.english: Is that so?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי אָמַר:
phrases.english: But when Rav Dimi came, he said:
There was an incident where a fox clawed a ewe
in the bathhouse of Beit Hini,
and the incident came before the Sages,
and they said: It is clawing!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי? וְהָא כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling in Step 13
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that a fox has no דרוסה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The חכמים ruled in a real case that a fox's clawing was דרוסה

steps.title: It was really a cat
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא answers that the animal in רב דימי's story was a cat, not a fox.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא said: that animal was really a cat.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ספרא saves רב כהנא's ruling by changing the facts of the story. The attacker was a cat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We already learned in Steps 6–7 that a cat can have דרוסה, so the חכמים' ruling makes sense. The story no longer has anything to do with foxes, and the ruling that a fox has no דרוסה stays in place.

phrases.english: Rav Safra said:
That one was a cat.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב סָפְרָא: הָהִיא חָתוּל הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 14
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-identifying the animal in the story
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The story shows that a fox has דרוסה
steps.terutzMaskana: The attacker was a cat, which does have דרוסה, so a fox still has none

steps.title: Second version: a fox does have דרוסה
steps.stepSummary: In another version, רב כהנא quotes רב שימי בר אשי as ruling the opposite: a fox does have דרוסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רב כהנא said in the name of רב שימי בר אשי that a fox does have דרוסה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another version of the whole exchange, where רב כהנא's ruling is reversed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There were two traditions about what רב שימי בר אשי said. In this version a fox's clawing counts, so the challenge that follows will be the opposite of the one in Step 14.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect, forbidden to eat

steps.confusionAlert: Steps 16–18 are not a new argument. They are the same exchange told in an opposite version, so don't mix up which ruling belongs to which version.

phrases.english: There are those who say:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Kahana said in the name of Rav Shimi bar Ashi:
A fox does have clawing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: An opposite version of Step 13
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A fox's clawing makes an animal a טריפה

steps.title: The same story, where the fox did not count
steps.stepSummary: In this version, the חכמים in רב דימי's story ruled that the fox's clawing was not דרוסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really? But רב דימי said: a fox clawed a sheep in the bathhouse of בית היני, and the חכמים said it is not דרוסה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the second version of the ruling with the same story, but here the חכמים say the clawing does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version the story shows the opposite: the חכמים ruled a fox's clawing is not דרוסה. That contradicts the ruling that a fox has דרוסה.

keyTerms.meaning: A place name, where the bathhouse was

phrases.english: Is that so?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי אָמַר:
phrases.english: But when Rav Dimi came, he said:
There was an incident where a fox clawed a ewe
in the bathhouse of Beit Hini,
and the incident came before the Sages,
and they said: It is not clawing!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי? וְהָא כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling in Step 16
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that a fox has דרוסה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The חכמים ruled in a real case that a fox's clawing was not דרוסה

steps.title: It was really a dog
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא answers that in this version, the animal in the story was a dog, not a fox.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא said: that animal was really a dog.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ספרא saves the second version of the ruling by saying the attacker was a dog.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A dog has no דרוסה, so the חכמים were right to say it did not count. The story is about a dog, so the ruling that a fox has דרוסה stays in place.

phrases.english: Rav Safra said:
That one was a dog.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב סָפְרָא: הָהוּא כֶּלֶב הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 17
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-identifying the animal in the story
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The story shows that a fox has no דרוסה
steps.terutzMaskana: The attacker was a dog, which has no דרוסה, so a fox still has it

steps.title: A tradition that a dog has no דרוסה
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף confirms that, by tradition, a dog has no דרוסה. This supports רב ספרא's answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: we have a tradition that a dog has no דרוסה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף backs up רב ספרא. A dog's clawing really does not count, so the חכמים' ruling fits a dog.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ספרא's answer only works if a dog has no דרוסה. רב יוסף confirms this with a received tradition, which closes this version of the exchange.

keyTerms.meaning: A dog's clawing does not count

steps.whatToRemember: There are two versions about the fox. In one, it has no דרוסה, and the story was about a cat. In the other, it has דרוסה, and the story was about a dog. Either way: a cat has דרוסה, and a dog does not.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
We have a tradition that a dog does not have clawing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: נָקְטִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב ספרא's answer in Step 18
steps.raayaObject: רב ספרא's claim that the story's ruling fits a dog
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב יוסף's received tradition that a dog has no דרוסה

steps.title: Four rules for what counts as דרוסה
steps.stepSummary: אביי lists four conditions for real דרוסה: with the front leg, with the claw, on purpose, and while the attacker is alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: we have a tradition. דרוסה is only with the front leg, not the back leg. It is only with the claw, not the tooth. It is only on purpose, not by accident. And it is only while the attacker is alive, not after it died.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a new, general definition of דרוסה with four conditions. Each one rules out a certain kind of attack.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the סוגיא asked which animals have דרוסה. אביי now asks how the attack must happen. Even an animal that has דרוסה makes its victim a טריפה only if all four conditions are met.
steps.whatToRemember: Real דרוסה needs all four: front leg, claw, on purpose, and a living attacker.
steps.whyThisMatters: These four conditions decide in practice when an attacked animal becomes a טריפה, whatever kind of predator attacked it.

phrases.english: Abaye said: We have a tradition:
Clawing is only with the foreleg,
phrases.notes: Literally 'the hand', meaning the animal's front leg.

phrases.english: to exclude the hind leg, which does not count.
Clawing is only with the claw,
to exclude the tooth, which does not count.
Clawing is only when done intentionally,
to exclude when done unintentionally, which does not count.
Clawing is only while the attacker is alive,
to exclude after its death, which does not count.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: נָקְטִינַן, אֵין דְּרוּסָה אֶלָּא בַּיָּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from which animals have דרוסה to how the attack must happen
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דרוסה counts only with the front leg, with the claw, on purpose, and while the attacker is alive

steps.title: Why say that clawing after death does not count?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why אביי's fourth condition, that the attacker must be alive, is needed at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: You already said that clawing without intent does not count. Is it even necessary to say that clawing after death does not count?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions one of אביי's four conditions for דרוסה. It looks extra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If clawing without intent is not דרוסה, then clawing by a dead animal is surely not דרוסה, since a dead animal has no intent at all. So the condition 'while alive' seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: is it necessary to say? (it should be obvious)

phrases.english: They say:
Now, about clawing without intent,
you said it does not count,
then about after death, is it even necessary to say?

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשְׁתָּא שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעַת אָמְרַתְּ לָא, לְאַחַר מִיתָה מִיבַּעְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אביי's list in step 20 because one condition looks unnecessary.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's fourth condition, that the attacker must be alive
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: קל וחומר logic: if clawing without intent does not count, clawing after death certainly does not count, so the condition adds nothing.

steps.title: The case of a paw cut off mid-attack
steps.stepSummary: The condition is needed for a case where the attacker clawed while alive, but its paw was cut off before it pulled its claws out.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where the animal clawed and its paw was cut off. You might have thought the venom goes in while it claws. He teaches us that the venom goes in while it pulls its claws out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what new case 'while alive' covers. It is a paw cut off while the claws are still stuck in the prey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attacker was alive and meant to claw, so the first three conditions are met. The new point is that the venom only goes in when the claws are pulled out. If the paw was cut off before that, no venom went in, and the prey is not a טריפה.

keyTerms.meaning: no, it is needed for a different case
you might have said (the wrong idea we would have had)

steps.confusionAlert: 'After death' here does not mean a dead animal clawing. It means the claws were already in, and then the paw was cut off before they came out.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where it clawed, and they cut off its paw.
phrases.notes: The claws are still stuck inside the prey when the paw is cut off.

phrases.english: You might have said:
while it claws, it releases its venom,
he teaches us:
while it pulls out, it releases its venom.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּדָרֵיס וּפַסְקוּהָ לִידֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 21 by finding a case the condition is needed for.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a new case (לא צריכא) where the condition teaches something new
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Venom goes in at the moment of clawing, so a cut-off paw would still make the prey a טריפה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Venom goes in only when the claws are pulled out, so if the paw was cut off first, it is not דרוסה.
steps.whatToRemember: Venom enters when the claws are pulled out, not when they go in.

steps.title: A lion among oxen and a claw in one ox's back
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that if a lion came among oxen and a claw is found in one ox's back, we do not worry that the lion clawed it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא said in the name of רב: If a lion came in among the oxen, and a claw was found in the back of one of them, we do not worry that the lion clawed it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching begins. רב gives a ruling about a suspicious claw found in an ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though a lion was there and a claw is stuck in the ox, רב says the ox is not treated as clawed. The גמרא will explain why next.

keyTerms.meaning: we do not worry, we do not take it into account

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna said in the name of Rav:
A lion that came in among the oxen,
and a claw was found in the back
of one of them,
we do not worry that maybe the lion clawed it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר רַב: אֲרִי שֶׁנִּכְנַס לְבֵין הַשְּׁוָורִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about doubtful דרוסה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A claw found in an ox's back after a lion was among the oxen does not make us suspect דרוסה.

steps.title: The reason: a lion that claws keeps its claw
steps.stepSummary: Most lions claw, but a lion that claws does not lose its claw. So a claw stuck in the ox suggests the ox rubbed against a wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? Most lions claw and a few do not. But any lion that claws does not lose its claw. Since this ox has a claw sitting in its back, say it rubbed against a wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for רב's reason and explains it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since most lions claw, we might suspect the lion attacked. But a clawing lion keeps its claws, so a loose claw stuck in the ox does not fit a lion attack. It fits better with the ox rubbing against a wall that had a claw stuck in it.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Most lions claw,
and a few of them do not claw,
and any lion that claws, its claw does not come out,

phrases.aramaic: וְזֹאת, הוֹאִיל וְצִפּוֹרֶן יוֹשֶׁבֶת לוֹ בְּגַבּוֹ –
phrases.english: and this one, since a claw is sitting in its back,
say it rubbed against a wall.
phrases.notes: He means a wall that had a claw stuck in it, which then got caught in the ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא? רוֹב אֲרָיוֹת דּוֹרְסִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason behind רב's ruling in step 23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why do we not suspect the lion clawed the ox?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A clawing lion keeps its claws, so a loose claw in the ox points to rubbing against a wall.

steps.title: On the contrary: the same logic points to the lion
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns the logic around. Most oxen rub against walls, but rubbing does not leave a claw in the back, so maybe the lion did claw it.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! Most oxen rub and a few do not. But any ox that rubs does not end up with a claw sitting in its back. Since this one has a claw in its back, say the lion clawed it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reason by using the exact same kind of argument in the other direction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rubbing is common, but rubbing usually does not leave a claw stuck in the ox. So the claw does not fit rubbing either, and it could point back to the lion. The two arguments now cancel each other out.

keyTerms.meaning: on the contrary, just the opposite

phrases.english: On the contrary,
most oxen rub themselves,
and a few of them do not rub,

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל הַמִּתְחַכֵּךְ – אֵין צִפּוֹרֶן יוֹשֶׁבֶת לוֹ בְּגַבּוֹ,
phrases.english: and any ox that rubs, no claw sits in its back,

phrases.aramaic: וְזֶה, הוֹאִיל וְצִפּוֹרֶן יוֹשֶׁבֶת לוֹ בְּגַבּוֹ,
phrases.english: and this one, since a claw is sitting in its back,
say the lion clawed it!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְּרַבָּה, רוֹב שְׁוָורִים מִתְחַכְּכִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning of step 24 by flipping it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason that the claw points to rubbing against a wall
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same 'majority but not this case' logic works for oxen rubbing, so the claw could just as well point to the lion.

steps.title: A tie, so the ox keeps its status
steps.stepSummary: Both arguments are equally strong, so we leave the ox in its default status. That makes it a case of ספק דרוסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can argue this way, and you can argue that way. So leave the ox in its default status. This is a case of doubtful clawing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits that both sides are equal and settles it with the ox's default status.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two majority arguments cancel out, so they prove nothing. We fall back on the ox's חזקה, its starting state of being healthy and kosher. The case is a ספק דרוסה, a doubt whether it was clawed.

keyTerms.meaning: leave it in its default status (חזקה)
a doubt whether an animal was clawed

phrases.english: One can argue this way,
and one can argue that way,
so leave the ox in its default status,
phrases.notes: Some versions say 'the matter' in round brackets; the square brackets give the corrected word, 'the ox'.

phrases.english: it is a case of doubtful clawing;

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר הָכִי, וְאִיכָּא לְמֵימַר הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 25 by accepting that the arguments are equal and turning to חזקה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Concedes a tie and decides by the default status (חזקה)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The majority reasoning alone proves the claw came from the wall.
steps.terutzMaskana: The reasoning is balanced. The ox is a ספק דרוסה and keeps its default kosher status.

steps.title: רב follows his own known view
steps.stepSummary: רב's ruling fits his known view that we do not worry about a ספק דרוסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב follows his own reasoning, since he said: We do not worry about doubtful clawing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ties רב's ruling about the lion to a general rule he holds elsewhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the case is only a doubt, רב's known rule decides it: a ספק דרוסה is not treated as a טריפה. So the ox is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: following his own reasoning (as he said elsewhere)

steps.whatToRemember: When the clues point both ways, the ox stays in its חזקה. רב holds we do not worry about a ספק דרוסה, so the ox is permitted.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how a tie between two 'majority' arguments is settled by חזקה, and that רב treats doubtful clawing leniently.

phrases.english: And Rav follows his own reasoning,
as he said: We do not worry about doubtful clawing.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב לְטַעְמֵיהּ, דְּאָמַר: אֵין חוֹשְׁשִׁין לִסְפֵק דְּרוּסָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes step 26 by applying רב's general rule to the doubt.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ox is permitted, because it is only a ספק דרוסה and רב does not worry about a ספק דרוסה.

steps.title: Only an actual moist claw removes the worry
steps.stepSummary: אביי says רב's leniency applies only when an actual claw is found, and only if that claw is moist.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: רב's rule is only about a claw. If we find just the spot where a claw went in, we do worry. Even a claw only helps if it is moist. A dry claw can slip out of a lion's paw.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי is putting limits on רב's ruling from the last steps, showing exactly when a found claw proves the lion did not attack.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's logic was that a lion's claw does not come off, so a claw stuck in the ox must have come from the wall. That only works if a real claw is there and it was firmly attached. A dry claw can fall off a lion, so it no longer proves anything, and the worry of דרוסה comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: The spot or hole where a claw went in, with no claw left
We are concerned, so we must check
It slips out or comes loose

phrases.english: Abaye said:
We said this only about a claw,
phrases.notes: He means רב's rule that we don't worry when a claw is found in the ox.

phrases.english: but the spot of a claw — we are concerned.

phrases.aramaic: וְצִפּוֹרֶן נָמֵי לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא לַחָה,
phrases.english: And a claw too, we said this only when it is moist,
but a dry one — it happens that it slips out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא צִפּוֹרֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows רב's ruling, which was just explained, to specific situations.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only an actual, moist claw shows the lion did not attack. A claw-hole alone, or a dry claw, means we must worry.

steps.title: Several claws in a row bring back the worry
steps.stepSummary: אביי adds that even a moist claw helps only if there is one. Two or three claws lined up like a paw mean we worry.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even with a moist claw, the rule is only for one claw. If there are two or three, we worry, as long as they stand in a row like a lion's paw.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי adds one more limit to רב's rule: the number and arrangement of the claws.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One claw could easily come from rubbing against a wall. Two or three claws lined up exactly like a lion's paw look like a real lion attack, so we must worry. The worry applies only when they form that paw pattern.
steps.whatToRemember: רב's leniency works only for one moist claw. A claw-hole, a dry claw, or several claws lined up like a paw all mean we worry about דרוסה.

phrases.english: And a moist one too, we did not say this
except about one,
but two or three — we are concerned,
and that is when they stand in a row like its paw.
phrases.notes: 'Its paw' means the lion's paw: the claws are lined up the way a lion's claws sit.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלַחָה נָמֵי לָא אֲמַרַן, אֶלָּא חֲדָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues אביי's list of limits, adding a third one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two or three claws lined up like a lion's paw mean we worry about דרוסה.

steps.title: רב and שמואל argue about an uncertain clawing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא formally quotes the מחלוקת: רב says we do not worry about ספק דרוסה, and שמואל says we do.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: רב says we are not concerned about a doubtful clawing. שמואל says we are concerned about a doubtful clawing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now quotes the actual disagreement between רב and שמואל. Step 27 had only mentioned רב's side of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 27 said רב's claw ruling fits his view on ספק דרוסה. Here the גמרא spells out both sides. For רב, a doubtful clawing leaves the animal permitted without checking. For שמואל, the animal must be checked.

keyTerms.meaning: A case where we are unsure if a predator clawed the animal
An animal clawed by a predator, which makes it טריפה

phrases.english: It was stated:

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָמַר: אֵין חוֹשְׁשִׁין לִסְפֵק דְּרוּסָה,
phrases.english: Rav says: We are not concerned about a doubtful clawing,
and Shmuel says: We are concerned about a doubtful clawing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר: רַב אָמַר: אֵין חוֹשְׁשִׁין לִסְפֵק דְּרוּסָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Formally presents the מחלוקת that step 27 referred to.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: no concern for ספק דרוסה. שמואל: we must worry and check.

steps.title: Everyone agrees: no worry if it may not have entered, or may have been a dog
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins listing cases where even שמואל agrees there is no worry. If we don't know whether a predator came in, we say it didn't. If we don't know whether it was a dog or a cat, we say it was a dog.
steps.simpleTranslation: Everyone agrees: if we are unsure whether it came in or not, we say it did not come in. If we are unsure whether it was a dog or a cat, we say it was a dog.
steps.whatsHappening: Before explaining what רב and שמואל argue about, the גמרא sets up the cases where they agree. That will narrow down the real disagreement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These doubts are too far back for anyone to worry. If we don't even know a predator was there, we assume it wasn't. If we don't know which animal it was, we assume the one whose clawing does not cause טריפה. So the מחלוקת must be about a more specific case.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean שמואל changed his mind. These are cases outside the מחלוקת, where even שמואל agrees there is no worry.

phrases.english: Everyone agrees:
if it is uncertain whether it entered or did not enter —
phrases.notes: "It" means a predator that might have come into the pen.

phrases.english: I say it did not enter.
if it is uncertain whether it was a dog or a cat —
I say it was a dog.
phrases.notes: We pick the dog because, for these animals, a dog's clawing does not make them טריפה.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא, סָפֵק עָל, סָפֵק לָא עָל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts defining the limits of the רב and שמואל מחלוקת by listing agreed cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a doubt whether a predator entered, or whether it was a dog or a cat, everyone agrees we are lenient.

steps.title: Everyone agrees: a quiet, calmed, or just noisy predator
steps.stepSummary: More agreed cases. A predator that sat quietly made peace. One that killed one animal calmed down. Roaring and clucking are only scaring.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it came in and sat quietly among them, I say it made peace. If it cut off the head of one of them, its anger calmed down. If it was roaring and they were clucking, they were just scaring.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps listing cases where everyone agrees we don't worry, even though the predator was surely inside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even when the predator definitely came in, certain signs show it did not claw the others. It sat calmly, or its anger was used up on one victim, or the noise was only fear and not an attack. In all these cases we assume no clawing happened.

phrases.english: If it entered, was quiet, and sat among them —
I say it made peace.
If it cut off the head of one of them —
its anger calmed down.
If it was roaring and they were clucking —
they are just scaring

steps.triggerLanguage: עָל, שְׁתֵיק וְיָתֵיב בֵּינַיְיהוּ – אֵימַר שְׁלָמָא שַׁוִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of cases where everyone agrees, now for cases where the predator definitely entered.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even if a predator entered, we assume no clawing if it sat quietly, killed only one, or only made frightening noise.
